1	# TIOBE Programming Community Index -- March 2026 Monthly Report
2	
3	## Source
4	
5	- URL: https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/
6	- Captured: April 10, 2026
7	- Author: Paul Jansen, CEO, TIOBE Software
8	
9	The TIOBE Programming Community Index is a widely cited indicator of programming language popularity, updated monthly since 2001. Ratings are calculated from the number of skilled engineers worldwide, training courses, and third-party vendors, using search-engine hit counts across Google, Amazon, Wikipedia, Bing, and more than 20 other sites. The index does not measure which language is "best" or which has the most lines of code written; rather, it reflects how much a language is discussed and sought after on the public internet.
10	
11	## March 2026 Headline: Why the TIOBE Index Still Relies on Search Engines
12	
13	The March 2026 editorial addresses a recurring question: should the TIOBE index switch from search-engine hit counts to LLM-based assessments of language popularity? Paul Jansen explains that the answer is no. LLMs are ultimately trained on the same web pages that search engines index, so querying an LLM would not yield fundamentally different data. The methodology therefore remains anchored to direct measurement of web-page volume per language.
14	
15	Beyond the methodology discussion, the March update records several notable rank changes. SQL and R swapped positions within the top 10, with R climbing from 16th to 9th year-over-year. Swift re-entered the top 20 at the expense of Kotlin, and Ruby is on the verge of dropping out of the top 30.
16	
17	## Top 20 Programming Languages -- March 2026
18	
19	![Top 20 programming languages ranked by TIOBE rating, March 2026](./assets/table_top20_rankings.jpg)
20	
21	| Rank (Mar 2026) | Rank (Mar 2025) | Programming Language | Rating | YoY Change |
22	|:---:|:---:|------|:---:|:---:|
23	| 1 | 1 | Python | 21.25% | -2.59% |
24	| 2 | 4 | C | 11.55% | +2.02% |
25	| 3 | 2 | C++ | 8.18% | -2.90% |
26	| 4 | 3 | Java | 7.99% | -2.37% |
27	| 5 | 5 | C# | 6.36% | +1.49% |
28	| 6 | 6 | JavaScript | 3.45% | -0.01% |
29	| 7 | 9 | Visual Basic | 2.50% | -0.02% |
30	| 8 | 8 | SQL | 2.00% | -0.57% |
31	| 9 | 16 | R | 1.88% | +0.94% |
32	| 10 | 10 | Delphi/Object Pascal | 1.80% | -0.36% |
33	| 11 | 24 | Perl | 1.75% | +1.05% |
34	| 12 | 12 | Scratch | 1.63% | -0.03% |
35	| 13 | 11 | Fortran | 1.45% | -0.25% |
36	| 14 | 14 | Rust | 1.31% | +0.09% |
37	| 15 | 15 | MATLAB | 1.29% | +0.31% |
38	| 16 | 7 | Go | 1.29% | -1.49% |
39	| 17 | 17 | Assembly language | 1.29% | +0.42% |
40	| 18 | 13 | PHP | 1.23% | -0.25% |
41	| 19 | 18 | Ada | 1.10% | +0.25% |
42	| 20 | 26 | Swift | 1.04% | +0.44% |
43	
44	Python holds the top position at 21.25%, more than double the rating of second-place C (11.55%). However, Python's year-over-year change is -2.59 percentage points, while C gained +2.02 points. The top 4 languages -- Python, C, C++, and Java -- collectively account for nearly 49% of the total index.
45	
46	## Historical Trend: Two Decades of Language Popularity (2002--2026)
47	
48	![Historical popularity trends for the top 10 programming languages from 2002 to 2026](./assets/chart_historical_trends.jpg)
49	
50	The TIOBE index publishes a long-running trend chart covering the top 10 languages from 2002 to the present. Key patterns visible in the data:
51	
52	- **Python's meteoric rise**: From a minor language ranked around 8th in 2006, Python surged to the top position after 2018, peaking above 25% before settling at 21.25% in March 2026.
53	- **C's resilience**: C has held a top-2 position for most of the 24-year span, with periodic surges (notably around 2015 and again in 2025--2026).
54	- **Java's long decline**: Java dominated the index from roughly 2005 to 2018, but has steadily fallen from the 25%+ range to under 8%.
55	- **JavaScript's plateau**: Despite its dominance in web development, JavaScript has never exceeded roughly 5% on the TIOBE index and currently sits at 3.45%.
56	
57	## Very Long Term History: Rank Positions Across Four Decades
58	
59	![Long-term ranking history of selected programming languages from 1986 to 2026](./assets/table_long_term_history.jpg)
60	
61	| Language | 2026 | 2021 | 2016 | 2011 | 2006 | 2001 | 1996 | 1991 | 1986 |
62	|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
63	| Python | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 8 | 26 | 17 | - | - |
64	| C | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
65	| C++ | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 9 |
66	| Java | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 31 | - | - |
67	| C# | 5 | 5 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 11 | - | - | - |
68	| JavaScript | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 10 | 8 | 33 | - | - |
69	| Go | 10 | 11 | 60 | 16 | - | - | - | - | - |
70	| Ada | 14 | 36 | 25 | 22 | 16 | 18 | 6 | 10 | 3 |
71	| Lisp | 26 | 34 | 26 | 13 | 14 | 19 | 8 | 4 | 2 |
72	
73	This table reveals dramatic shifts across decades. Python was unranked before 1991, entered the top 30 only by 2001, and took 25 years to reach the top position. Conversely, Lisp was the number-2 language in 1986 but has fallen to 26th. Ada peaked at 3rd in 1986 and now sits at 14th. C is the only language that has remained in the top 2 across all nine measurement points.
74	
75	## Programming Language Hall of Fame
76	
77	![Hall of Fame -- Language of the Year winners from 2003 to 2025](./assets/table_hall_of_fame.jpg)
78	
79	The TIOBE "Programming Language of the Year" award goes to the language with the largest gain in ratings during a calendar year. Recent winners include:
80	
81	| Year | Winner |
82	|:---:|------|
83	| 2025 | C# |
84	| 2024 | Python |
85	| 2023 | C# |
86	| 2022 | C++ |
87	| 2021 | Python |
88	| 2020 | Python |
89	| 2019 | C |
90	| 2018 | Python |
91	| 2016 | Go |
92	
93	Python has won the award five times (2007, 2010, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024), more than any other language. C# took the title in both 2023 and 2025, reflecting its continued growth driven by the .NET ecosystem.
94	
95	## Key Findings
96	
97	- **Python remains dominant but is losing ground**: At 21.25%, Python leads by a wide margin, yet its year-over-year decline of -2.59 percentage points is the largest drop among the top 5. C, by contrast, gained +2.02 points and climbed from 4th to 2nd.
98	- **Legacy languages show surprising resilience**: Perl jumped from 24th to 11th (+1.05%), R rose from 16th to 9th (+0.94%), and Fortran remains in the top 15. These languages continue to serve entrenched communities in scientific computing, data analysis, and infrastructure.
99	- **Go suffers its sharpest decline**: Go fell from 7th to 16th, losing 1.49 percentage points -- the largest absolute drop of any top-20 language. This contrasts with its 2016 "Language of the Year" win and suggests possible displacement by Rust (14th, +0.09%) in the systems programming space.
100	- **Swift re-enters the top 20, Kotlin exits**: Swift climbed from 26th to 20th (+0.44%), while Kotlin dropped to 22nd. In the mobile development ecosystem, Swift's gains may reflect Apple platform growth, while Kotlin faces competition from cross-platform frameworks.
101	- **The top 4 languages hold nearly half the index**: Python, C, C++, and Java together account for 48.97% of total TIOBE ratings, illustrating how concentrated the programming landscape remains despite 50+ tracked languages.
102

# TIOBE Programming Community Index -- March 2026 Monthly Report

## Source

- URL: https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/
- Captured: April 10, 2026
- Author: Paul Jansen, CEO, TIOBE Software

The TIOBE Programming Community Index is a widely cited indicator of programming language popularity, updated monthly since 2001. Ratings are calculated from the number of skilled engineers worldwide, training courses, and third-party vendors, using search-engine hit counts across Google, Amazon, Wikipedia, Bing, and more than 20 other sites. The index does not measure which language is "best" or which has the most lines of code written; rather, it reflects how much a language is discussed and sought after on the public internet.

## March 2026 Headline: Why the TIOBE Index Still Relies on Search Engines

The March 2026 editorial addresses a recurring question: should the TIOBE index switch from search-engine hit counts to LLM-based assessments of language popularity? Paul Jansen explains that the answer is no. LLMs are ultimately trained on the same web pages that search engines index, so querying an LLM would not yield fundamentally different data. The methodology therefore remains anchored to direct measurement of web-page volume per language.

Beyond the methodology discussion, the March update records several notable rank changes. SQL and R swapped positions within the top 10, with R climbing from 16th to 9th year-over-year. Swift re-entered the top 20 at the expense of Kotlin, and Ruby is on the verge of dropping out of the top 30.

## Top 20 Programming Languages -- March 2026

| 2021 | Python |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build the TIOBE Index March 2026 data analysis deck."""

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt, Emu
from pptx.dml.color import RGBColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE, XL_LEGEND_POSITION, XL_LABEL_POSITION

SLIDE_WIDTH = Inches(13.333)
SLIDE_HEIGHT = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette - professional, data-forward
NAVY = RGBColor(0x1B, 0x2A, 0x4A)
DARK_BLUE = RGBColor(0x2C, 0x3E, 0x6B)
ACCENT_BLUE = RGBColor(0x3B, 0x82, 0xF6)
LIGHT_BLUE = RGBColor(0xDB, 0xEA, 0xFE)
WHITE = RGBColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
LIGHT_GRAY = RGBColor(0xF1, 0xF5, 0xF9)
MED_GRAY = RGBColor(0x94, 0xA3, 0xB8)
DARK_GRAY = RGBColor(0x47, 0x55, 0x69)
TEXT_DARK = RGBColor(0x1E, 0x29, 0x3B)
GREEN = RGBColor(0x16, 0xA3, 0x4A)
RED = RGBColor(0xDC, 0x26, 0x26)
AMBER = RGBColor(0xF5, 0x9E, 0x0B)
TEAL = RGBColor(0x0D, 0x94, 0x88)
PURPLE = RGBColor(0x7C, 0x3A, 0xED)


def set_slide_bg(slide, color):
    bg = slide.background
    fill = bg.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color


def add_shape_with_fill(slide, left, top, width, height, color, corner_radius=None):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, left, top, width, height)
    shape.fill.solid()
    shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = color
    shape.line.fill.background()
    if corner_radius is not None:
        shape.adjustments[0] = corner_radius
    return shape


def set_text(shape, text, font_size=12, bold=False, color=TEXT_DARK, alignment=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri"):
    tf = shape.text_frame
    tf.clear()
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = Pt(font_size)
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = alignment
    return tf


def add_text_box(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=12, bold=False, color=TEXT_DARK, alignment=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri"):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = Pt(font_size)
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = alignment
    return txBox


def add_paragraph(tf, text, font_size=12, bold=False, color=TEXT_DARK, alignment=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, space_before=Pt(4), font_name="Calibri"):
    p = tf.add_paragraph()
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = Pt(font_size)
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = alignment
    if space_before:
        p.space_before = space_before
    return p


# ── Slide builders ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

def build_slide_1_title(prs):
    """Title slide."""
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])  # blank
    set_slide_bg(slide, NAVY)

    # Decorative accent bar at top
    bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), SLIDE_WIDTH, Inches(0.08))
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT_BLUE
    bar.line.fill.background()

    # Main title
    add_text_box(slide, Inches(1.2), Inches(1.8), Inches(11), Inches(1.6),
                 "TIOBE Index March 2026",
                 font_size=42, bold=True, color=WHITE, font_name="Calibri")

    add_text_box(slide, Inches(1.2), Inches(3.2), Inches(11), Inches(1.2),
                 "How 20+ Search Engines Rank the World's Programming Languages",
                 font_size=24, bold=False, color=RGBColor(0xBF, 0xDB, 0xFE), font_name="Calibri")

    # Methodology box
    mbox = add_shape_with_fill(slide, Inches(1.2), Inches(4.6), Inches(7.5), Inches(1.6),
                                RGBColor(0x23, 0x3A, 0x5F), 0.02)
    tf = mbox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = "METHODOLOGY"
    p.font.size = Pt(10)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = ACCENT_BLUE
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    add_paragraph(tf, "Ratings are calculated from skilled-engineer counts, training courses, and third-party vendor data using search-engine hit counts across Google, Bing, Wikipedia, Amazon, and 20+ other sites.",
                  font_size=12, color=RGBColor(0xCB, 0xD5, 0xE1), font_name="Calibri")

    # Audience tag
    add_text_box(slide, Inches(1.2), Inches(6.6), Inches(6), Inches(0.4),
                 "For Software Engineering Leads & Technology Strategists",
                 font_size=11, color=MED_GRAY, font_name="Calibri")

    # Date tag
    add_text_box(slide, Inches(9.5), Inches(6.6), Inches(3), Inches(0.4),
                 "Source: tiobe.com  |  March 2026",
                 font_size=11, color=MED_GRAY, alignment=PP_ALIGN.RIGHT, font_name="Calibri")

        (3, 2, "C++", "8.18%", -2.90),

        (6, 6, "JavaScript", "3.45%", -0.01),
        (7, 9, "Visual Basic", "2.50%", -0.02),
        (8, 8, "SQL", "2.00%", -0.57),
        (9, 16, "R", "1.88%", +0.94),
        (10, 10, "Delphi/Obj Pascal", "1.80%", -0.36),
        (11, 24, "Perl", "1.75%", +1.05),
        (12, 12, "Scratch", "1.63%", -0.03),
        (13, 11, "Fortran", "1.45%", -0.25),
        (14, 14, "Rust", "1.31%", +0.09),
        (15, 15, "MATLAB", "1.29%", +0.31),
        (16, 7, "Go", "1.29%", -1.49),
        (17, 17, "Assembly", "1.29%", +0.42),
        (18, 13, "PHP", "1.23%", -0.25),
        (19, 18, "Ada", "1.10%", +0.25),
        (20, 26, "Swift", "1.04%", +0.44),
    ]

    # Bar chart on the left using python-pptx chart
    chart_data = __import__('pptx').chart.data.CategoryChartData()
    chart_data.categories = [r[2] for r in rankings]
    chart_data.add_series('Rating %', [float(r[3].replace('%', '')) for r in rankings])

        Inches(0.3), Inches(1.15), Inches(6.4), Inches(6.1),

    chart.has_title = False

    # Style the chart

    plot.gap_width = 60
    series = plot.series[0]
    series.format.fill.solid()
    series.format.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT_BLUE

    top_colors = [RGBColor(0x1D, 0x4E, 0xD8), RGBColor(0x22, 0x63, 0xEB), ACCENT_BLUE, RGBColor(0x60, 0xA5, 0xFA), RGBColor(0x93, 0xBB, 0xFD)]
    for i in range(5):
        pt = series.points[i]
        pt.format.fill.solid()
        pt.format.fill.fore_color.rgb = top_colors[i]

    # Data labels
    series.has_data_labels = True
    series.data_labels.font.size = Pt(8)
    series.data_labels.font.color.rgb = DARK_GRAY
    series.data_labels.number_format = '0.00"%"'
    series.data_labels.label_position = XL_LABEL_POSITION.OUTSIDE_END

    # Category axis
    cat_axis = chart.category_axis
    cat_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(8)
    cat_axis.tick_labels.font.color.rgb = TEXT_DARK
    cat_axis.has_major_gridlines = False
    cat_axis.major_tick_mark = 2  # outside

    val_axis = chart.value_axis
    val_axis.visible = False
    val_axis.has_major_gridlines = True
    val_axis.major_gridlines.format.line.color.rgb = RGBColor(0xE2, 0xE8, 0xF0)
    val_axis.major_gridlines.format.line.width = Pt(0.5)

    # Table on the right side
    rows = 21
    cols = 5
    tbl_shape = slide.shapes.add_table(rows, cols, Inches(7.0), Inches(1.15), Inches(6.0), Inches(6.1))
    table = tbl_shape.table

    col_widths = [Inches(0.7), Inches(0.7), Inches(2.0), Inches(1.1), Inches(1.1)]
    for i, w in enumerate(col_widths):
        table.columns[i].width = w

    headers = ["2026", "2025", "Language", "Rating", "YoY"]
    for ci, h in enumerate(headers):
        cell = table.cell(0, ci)
        cell.text = h
        for p in cell.text_frame.paragraphs:
            p.font.size = Pt(9)
            p.font.bold = True
            p.font.color.rgb = WHITE
            p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER
            p.font.name = "Calibri"
        cell.fill.solid()
        cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = NAVY
        cell.vertical_anchor = MSO_ANCHOR.MIDDLE

    for ri, (rank, prev, lang, rating, yoy) in enumerate(rankings):
        row_idx = ri + 1
        yoy_str = f"+{yoy:.2f}%" if yoy >= 0 else f"{yoy:.2f}%"
        vals = [str(rank), str(prev), lang, rating, yoy_str]
        for ci, val in enumerate(vals):
            cell = table.cell(row_idx, ci)
            cell.text = val
            for p in cell.text_frame.paragraphs:
                p.font.size = Pt(8.5)
                p.font.name = "Calibri"
                p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER if ci != 2 else PP_ALIGN.LEFT
                if ci == 4:
                    p.font.color.rgb = GREEN if yoy >= 0 else RED
                    p.font.bold = True
                else:
                    p.font.color.rgb = TEXT_DARK
            cell.vertical_anchor = MSO_ANCHOR.MIDDLE
            # Alternating row colors
            if ri % 2 == 0:
                cell.fill.solid()
                cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = RGBColor(0xF8, 0xFA, 0xFC)
            else:
                cell.fill.solid()
                cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = WHITE

    # Callout: top 4 = 49%
    callout = add_shape_with_fill(slide, Inches(7.0), Inches(0.95), Inches(6.0), Inches(0.18),
                                   LIGHT_BLUE, 0.0)
    set_text(callout, " Top 4 languages (Python, C, C++, Java) hold 48.97% of total index ratings",
             font_size=8, bold=True, color=DARK_BLUE, alignment=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

        ("R", "16th \u2192 9th", "+7 ranks", "+0.94%", "Growing demand in data science & statistical computing; complementing Python in analytics workflows"),

        ("C", "4th \u2192 2nd", "+2 ranks", "+2.02%", "Largest absolute rating gain among top 20; resilient systems language surges past C++ and Java"),
